overshoot.description: Signal overshoots the settled high level after a rising transition
possible_causes: Impedance mismatch between source and transmission line
Underdamped LC response (parasitic inductance + load capacitance)
Long PCB trace acting as a transmission line at fast edge speeds
Probe compensation error introducing artificial overshoot
suggestions: Add a series termination resistor (typically 22–100 Ω) close to the driver output
Match source impedance to the line impedance (typically 50 Ω)
Check and adjust probe compensation with a 1 kHz calibration square wave
Reduce trace length or use controlled-impedance routing
Add a small series resistor (10–33 Ω) to damp high-frequency ringing

undershoot.description: Signal undershoots the settled low level after a falling transition
possible_causes: Same root causes as overshoot — impedance mismatch on the falling edge
Inductive kickback from a load (motor, relay, inductor)
Negative ringing from reflected signal on long traces
suggestions: Add a series termination resistor near the source
For inductive loads: add a flyback diode (freewheeling diode) across the load
Reduce switching speed if not timing-critical (slower slew rate = less ringing)

ringing.description: Damped sinusoidal oscillation superimposed on the signal after a transition
possible_causes: Resonance between parasitic trace inductance and load/stray capacitance
Transmission line unterminated or improperly terminated
Via or connector discontinuity causing impedance mismatch
Probe ground lead too long (adds inductance)
suggestions: Use a series damping resistor (22–100 Ω) at the driver output
Shorten probe ground lead or use a ground spring
Match line impedance with proper termination
Use ground planes and minimize loop areas in the PCB layout

jitter.description: Cycle-to-cycle timing variation — the period is not perfectly consistent
possible_causes: Electromagnetic interference (EMI) coupling into the signal
Power supply noise modulating the switching threshold
PLL/clock source instability
Insufficient ground plane or poor PCB layout
Thermal noise at low signal amplitudes
suggestions: Improve shielding and reduce EMI sources near the signal path
Add bulk and high-frequency decoupling capacitors to the power rails
Check PLL loop filter if using a synthesized clock
Increase signal amplitude if it is close to noise floor
Improve PCB ground plane continuity

noise.description: High-frequency random variation superimposed on the signal
possible_causes: EMI pickup from nearby switching supplies, motors, or RF sources
Ground loop — multiple ground paths with different potentials
Insufficient high-frequency decoupling on power rails
Poor signal routing (long parallel runs next to switching signals)
Thermal noise (Johnson–Nyquist noise) in high-impedance circuits
suggestions: Add 100 nF ceramic bypass capacitors close to every IC power pin
Use a solid, uninterrupted ground plane
Route sensitive signals away from switching power or clock signals
Use differential signaling if noise margin is insufficient
Shield the signal path if EMI is from external sources

ripple.description: Low-frequency periodic variation superimposed on an otherwise DC signal
possible_causes: Insufficient output capacitance on the power supply
Switching frequency ripple from a DC-DC converter
Line frequency (50/60 Hz) hum from an unfiltered AC-DC supply
Shared return path causing load current modulation
suggestions: Increase output filter capacitance (bulk electrolytic + ceramic in parallel)
Add a post-regulation LC filter at the load
Use a linear regulator (LDO) after the switching supply for noise-sensitive circuits
Ensure good ground plane continuity to minimize shared impedance

clipping.description: Signal peak is abnormally flat, indicating saturation or hard limiting
possible_causes: Amplifier output saturated (input signal too large)
Output voltage limited by supply rail (signal exceeds Vcc or GND)
Deliberate limiting/clipping in a protection circuit
ADC input range exceeded (digital clipping in acquisition hardware)
suggestions: Reduce input signal amplitude to keep the output within linear range
Check if the supply voltage is sufficient for the required output swing
Increase supply voltage if the circuit design allows
Verify the amplifier's output voltage specification vs. observed clipping level

slow_rise_time.description: Rise time is a significant fraction of the signal period
possible_causes: Excessive capacitive load on the driver output
Signal bandwidth intentionally or unintentionally limited by an RC filter
Driver output current limited (unable to charge load capacitance quickly)
Scope bandwidth set too low (an apparent rise time issue, not real)
suggestions: Reduce capacitive load or add a buffer between driver and load
Check scope bandwidth setting — should be at least 5× the signal frequency
Use a higher-current driver or buffer amplifier
If filtering is needed, use an intentional filter with a defined cutoff

dc_offset.description: Significant DC offset relative to the signal amplitude
possible_causes: Intentional DC bias (e.g., AC signal riding on a DC rail)
Leakage current through coupling capacitors
Scope probe input impedance interacting with the circuit
suggestions: Use AC coupling on the scope channel to view only the AC component
Check if the DC offset is expected for the circuit's operating point
Verify scope probe ground reference
